content: An odontogenic keratocyst is a benign but locally aggressive developmental cyst that originates from odontogenic tissues. It is believed to arise from remnants of the dental lamina. Typically, odontogenic keratocysts are asymptomatic, and pain is not commonly associated with them unless swelling or secondary infection occurs. These cysts most frequently involve the posterior region of the mandible. In cases where multiple odontogenic keratocysts are present, they are often associated with nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (NBCCS), also known as Gorlin-Goltz syndrome. In recent years, the term keratocystic odontogenic tumor (KCOT) has been adopted to describe these lesions, both in solitary cases and in those associated with syndromic conditions, as per the 2005 World Health Organization (WHO) classification. This terminology reflects the neoplastic potential of these lesions. Although rare, there have been reports of neoplastic transformation within odontogenic keratocysts. A small number of cases have documented the development of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) arising from these cysts. Additionally, there have been several cases of ameloblastic transformation occurring within the epithelial lining of odontogenic keratocysts.
